## Decision: * We will use an elastic index
* Elastic will be served by the backend, in memory
* Each task will be represented by a document
* Changes in tasks will be represented by events

We will use Elasticsearch, but not use the same index in the same `task`, because this would entail multiple
Elastic queries for updating each task. We will need to use different index for changes tasks. We will
also use some `changes` index in `task` for changes not covered by a specific task. We have two options,
`events` and `tasks` indexes (the current name of the tasks index).

The `TaskService` will use a `Task` and `Change` in both read and write operations, and change their
respective Elasticsearch indexes.

Elastic changes indexes:

* When adding a new change, a record is added at the end of the relevant `changes` index.
* When getting information from changes related to a given `task`, change is retrieved from changes index.
  
Elastic indexes for changes related to a given `Task`:

* When adding a change to a `task`, the `changes` index receives changes only done related to this change,
  related to `Task`.
* When adding more changes to a `task` that have already been recorded, changes are merged at the end of the
  `changes` index, i.e., all changes are appended there.
  
Changes indexes include the following fields:

* A `_id` field that contains the change IDs
* A `_version` field that stores the point in time of the changes
* A `_transform` field that describes the transformations applied
* An `_order` field that establishes a natural order
* A `changes` field that stores all the changes related to this particular change
* A `task_id` field that stores the ID of the `Task` that is concerned by changes

Related items in the changes index:

* [change-1.json](https://github.com/SpaceX/change-1.json)
* [change-2.json](https://github.com/SpaceX/change-2.json)
* [change-3.json](https://github.com/SpaceX/change-3.json)

## Decision: We have chosen to handle login actions as a 'web request' class using 301 Redirection rather than sending an
httpError. This causes the browser to send a GET request to the action via the WebAuthFlow. We allow
at most 2 minutes of the response time.

A 301 Redirection is a client redirect, initiated automatically by the browser. 
So, if we fail to complete an action, the client (user) browser will 
redirect back to a form or web url where we can again attempt the action.

It is useful to note that if this mechanism was not enabled by a browser, the 
request would be complete when we fail (when getting the 301), we would 
be forced to allow the browser, and the user would be able to authenticate
at its own convenience. We want to disallow this.

Note that any input used to login is treated as a POST or PUT request, 
and is sent along with the user session cookie.

## Decision: Separate out the build and runtime documentation from the framework documentation. The build and runtime documentation can be created alongside the code. Separate docs for build and runtime give us more control over the content and more ability to evolve them independently. 
Additionally, these docs can be checked into the repository as part of the build and runtime.

The runtime and build docs will be rendered in HTML and JavaScript, in a GitHub pages compatible format. This will allow them to be displayed in a UI as needed, be easily shared, and be updated asynchronously. 
The documentation will reside in a subdirectory of the repo. The structure of the files in this subdirectory is similar to the current documentation: a directory containing a subdirectory for each month, and all docs are stored under a directory for the particular year. 
Files that are only required for a single state of the framework should be placed in a subdirectory. 

```
.
├── build
│   ├── documentation
│   └── state
├── runtime
│   └── documentation
└── README.md
```

The build and runtime docs will be rendered using a local server. The tools required for this purpose will be stored in a separate repository. 
This separation of concerns will reduce our dependency on system-specific tooling, and improve portability across different environments.

## Decision: A lot of the assertions are dead codes.
A lot of assertions are unreachable and will never be hit.
You can ignore such assertions if they slow you down.
Also, as the assertions are unreachable, you won't be able to use `sassert`.

Assertions should be only used to assert that state of the environment
is as you expect it.
Assertions should stop the execution.

It is [useless to put assertions
in `d` statements](https://github.com/ElektraInitiative/elektra/issues/144)
because `d` statements are never reached.
Assertions thus cannot be used to ensure
that assertions are hit.
A non-obvious example for assertions is the
[State Tree format](https://github.com/ElektraInitiative/elektra/issues/160)
to store state.
The only way to ensure that assertions are hit is
by asserting all State Trees
exist and that all specific State Trees are hit.
However, the Assertion engine doesn't know this
and cannot do the work as it needs to check
that all specific State Trees are present.
Thus, you cannot put assertions in `d` statements
and expect the execution to stop at the desired point.
You still expect the execution to stop at the assertion,
but you don't know for sure.
Assertions are merely used to ensure
that State Trees are present.

## Decision: * superwerker should be able to use the unique AWS account root user email address and handle it securely
* the AWS root user should be allowed to access a given AWS account / Cloud Platform only if there is a Secure Environment (i.e. a private mailbox) with at least the same protection level as the Cloud Platform
* Root emails should not be shared
* As a minimum, the "root mail" should be set to a non-obvious address, for instance by putting a subdomain between the name and the domain. E.g. "root@example.account.domain.com"
* [The "root user mail"](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2018/09/enabling-imemail-authentication/): enable the imemail authentication method for root email users in AWS
* An "imemail" mailbox must be an AWS account root mailbox
* [Secure mailbox][securemail]: Configure the AWS root mailbox as a "Secure Mailbox", by enabling "Fail authentication at IMAP and SMTP" and setting the "Quoting style" to "Double quotes and newlines"
* A [root email][rootemail]: Use a *fixed length (of at least 64 bytes)* "Root Email Address", that is encoded as bytes and optionally appended with a `@` symbol.

### Notes:

- "root mail" is an alternative name given to a root email address
- We are only able to manage the first level of a hierarchical mailbox - subdomains are not taken into account
- The address strings must be UTF-8, length-limited to 255, and contain neither characters nor metacentrics not defined in the "ISO-8859-1" encoding. This matches [RFC 822][rfc822] which says "the entire message, as it will be encoded as the base-64 payload, must be UTF-8 encoded".
- If we add or use the `@` symbol in a mail address, we make it an encoded mail address and should use a `Content-Type` of `text/plain`
- [RFC 822][rfc822]: http://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc822
- [Double Newlines][dblnew]: A single new line character sequence

## Decision: We will store all sent messages into the
[ReferralRepository](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/beis-referral/blob/main/doc/architecture/patterns.md#referralrepository):

The key parts of messages are referred to as `messageId`.
Referrals may not have an ID if their draft has not been sent.
This needs a new feature.

When an event is recorded, the details are posted into the respective stack's queue.

The 5 main events are:

- draft sent (to remove draft draft messages)
- draft marked as sent (to mark draft as sent messages as sent)
- draft submitted (when we mark a draft as complete)
- message posted (when we post the message into the stack)
- commission updated (when we update the commission's data)
- intervention booked (when an intervention is booked)
- referral event submitted (these are custom fields)
- referral event marked as complete (these are custom fields)
- supplier assessment booked (when the first supplier assessment is booked)
- action plan submitted (when the first version of the action plan is submitted)

These are the events currently known for be recorded.

The intervention details in messages will be stored loosely, and can be pulled by data users as required.
Storing the full details of the interventions as defined at the moment would be difficult to support.

Interventions are not considered "private", as they will be in a shared component accessible to all users of the service, even if they differ between applications.

We will record each message as an event that contains the `messageId` and other metadata.
This will help users to access each message after the fact.

The messages are stored as a "time-space index" of the `messageId`.
All the events will have the `time-space index` as the ID.

This ensures that it's possible to get all events in a particular time-space index.
To be able to track the changes to a specific message, we will store all the messages that share the same `messageId`.
They will be stored under the "messages" directory.

In addition, each stack has a directory with the name of the system, where the messages are stored in a "message-registry".
This will map the `messageId` to the messages.

## Decision: * The URI's Tag (ontology) should be defined as much as possible at the highest level of the ontology
* The URI should contain domain, entity id and any ids at the lowest level of the hierarchy (e.g. url tags)
* The URI's namespace should be defined as a FQDN (example: https://www.monobilla.com/ontology/org)
* The URI should be resolvable
* The URI should be sustainable (persist data for as long as possible)
* The URI should be transparent, i.e., the individual parts of the URI should not be semantically meaningful
* The URI should be immutable
* The URI should be independent of the naming scheme of the individual parts
* The URI's tag/ontology should not be tagged as ontologically equivalent to any other in the same hierarchy or higher
* Tag URIs should use [the "Tag URI scheme](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc4151); e.g. `tag:<@ontology.id>`
* Tag URIs should only contain mandatory parts and allowed optional parts; e.g.
  * `tag:<@ontology.id>,<tag:version>`
  * `tag:<@ontology.id>,<tag:version>,<tag:language>`
  * `tag:<@ontology.id>,<tag:version>,<tag:language>,<tag:encoding>`
* The namespace should be resolvable
* The URI should be uniquely usable
* The URI should use the `org.w3c` prefix for the namespace (except when the namespace is not an ONS URI.)

## Decision: As per our policy, any SMS messaging must be able to be triggered by WhatsApp, and that any messaging system must also allow delivery of any SMS in English and Bangla. The reason is that both we and the patients must be able to use both languages. (This removes many non-Western SMS systems.)

The message we want to send via WhatsApp is the same message we would send via TextNow, but the latter supports SMS. We choose TextNow over Twilio because it's cheaper. Twilio is a free enterprise product, Twilio's customer base is very large, and we would be unable to leverage the shared infrastructure of Twilio with our system, as our domain structure is different. TextNow's customer base is relatively small, but we will be able to leverage their existing infrastructure with our system. Additionally, the Twilio development community is relatively smaller. Twilio offers several products, including Voice, SMS, Messaging, Signage, and Contact, and we would be responsible for managing multiple products.

Imo is a very popular messaging system in Bangladesh. Although the Imo API does not allow direct triggering of sending SMS via WhatsApp or Twilio, the developers of our React system and the developers of the Daktak mobile app have worked together in the past to develop a work-around using [Webhooks](https://developer.facebook.com/developers/docs/social/webgraph/webhooks) (see https://github.com/build-a-foundation/daktak/pull/166 and https://github.com/build-a-foundation/daktak-android/issues/48) whereby messages are sent via Facebook Messenger and then forwarded via Imo.

Although sending Facebook Messenger messages via Webhooks might be more work than using Twilio, the alternative - doing without messaging for the 80% of patients in Bangladesh who use Imo regularly - is not an option. Therefore, any solution must be able to send messages both via Facebook Messenger and via a text messaging API.

### Messaging through WhatsApp

* Send message via Twilio (or TextNow) API
* Translate the message to Bangla and English (using Google Translate)
* Send message via WhatsApp API

### Messaging through TextNow

* Send message via Twilio API
* Translate the message to Bangla and English (using Google Translate)
* Send message via TextNow API

Issue data is retrieved from the Archiver instance of the specified `ArchiverAccount`.
This instance must be a member of the AWS Organisation.
The deployment must be created from an existing AWS Organisation.
The deployment is specified by `Account.Environment.Name`.

### CloudWatch

Issue data is sent to [AWS CloudWatch](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/) to be issued
as time based alarms, which are used to ensure compliance deadlines are met.

### Lambda

Issue data is sent to [AWS Lambda](https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/) to be carried as a message to other AWS services.
Note that this usage implies that the issue has been resolved.

### Infrastructure as Code

This module supports "as-code" deployments.
The deployment infrastructure is specified via Github issues.
By convention, we refer to the issues as "Issues", "Issues-".
Issues are also used to test the functionality of the module.
A `.github-issue` suffix is added to issues in the repo that will be the issue.
`Issue#`-pre prefixed issue ids are also used.
The issue id is also used for all variable names.
As such, we require all issue ids to begin with `-` followed by all digits.
We also require all issue ids to be in the range 1,2,3,...9999-999,999.
The issue id is also used as the name of the S3 bucket to store all related resources.
This means that if the issue id is 1234, then the S3 bucket name will be `issue_1234`.

## Decision: ### Access for Federated Properties to local properties

#### Case 1: The Local API does not host a module for the particular local Property.

This is not a problem, because we just switch the local API to
access the "local" version of the Local Properties.

In addition, since we switch the local API off during the build process, and each module is loaded separately, we will never load an additional module for any local Property.

#### Case 2: The Local API hosts a module for the local Property.

Local API modules should be loaded and stored in the local wiki, because we don't want a separate build step. They also will not require any additional modules from our perspective.

All this requires to allow the use of Federated Properties is to use the local API module, and "enable" Federated Properties by switching off the local API. In addition, we must switch on Federated Properties using the API by setting the value of `wb_enable_federated_properties` to 1.

### Access for Federated Properties to remote properties

#### Case 1: The remote API does not host a module for the remote Property.

In this case, the remote Property can be retrieved either via the Remote API or the Federated Properties module in the local API (if it also has the remote module available).

#### Case 2: The remote API hosts a module for the remote Property.

This is the same as Case 1.
However, now the remote Property can be retrieved via the Federated Properties module.
In addition, we cannot switch this on during the build process, as it results in two modules for a single remote Property.

We need to use a different mechanism or keep one of the solutions.
The solutions are 1) not switching on the Federated Properties in the build process, and 2) switching on the Federated Properties in the build process.

### Switching on or off Federated Properties during the build process

Given that we can only do this once per remote Property, this means that no changes can be made to the build in two.
The build needs to be switched on in step 1, before the Remote Property.

We need to switch on the Federated Properties before the local Property in order to allow any of the local Properties to be used with the remote properties.

## Decision: We would like to introduce the concept of a LightClient for use in the "seed" mode of the LightNode.

### Background
[LiteClient](https://github.com/polychainlabs/light-client) and [Seed](https://github.com/polychainlabs/light-client/tree/master/p2p-seed-network) code is already available in the codebase.
Most of our light client code already exist at the infrastructure level, but not at a library level. 
For the sake of completeness, it should be mentioned that a `light-client` node is not capable of syncing with all networks and peers.
For example, to sync with a `tendermint` node, first `tendermint` should be completely synced. (100% downloaded, except for the headers)
This means that for syncing we use the `tendermint` `light-client` as the backbone of the chain synchronization.

### Assumptions
1. All the assumptions done in [ADR-020 LightClient in full node](./0020-light-client-in-full-node.md) are valid in the context of a light node.
2. Users of the Tendermint API can run a `light-client` node for use in the "seed" mode of the LightNode.
3. This `light-client` will be used only in the "seed" mode of the LightNode.
4. 100% of the Tendermint `light-client` is downloaded and verified.
5. Syncing with the Tendermint `light-client` network is done via the `Tendermint RPC`.

The above assumptions will require some changes in the code. Therefore we defer these assumptions and keep these as guidelines.

## Decision: We should disable user command logging in the cases of success and failure.

To enable such functionality we should adopt a `::echo::on` or `::echo::off` directive by command name (e.g., `::echo::off echo::on`: '::echo::off''). The order of enabling commands should be handled by the framework.

The `::echo::off` command should be used by the `::echo::on` command for switching the command behavior.

The default behavior of command echoing is to have the command output be seen by the user in both `kdb_get`, `elektra_get`, `kdb_set` or `elektra_set` log commands. This default behavior will be reversed for failure, when the command log output should be visible regardless of the success condition.

To be useful while debugging this feature, the `kdbSet` or `elektraSet` command should send the last few lines from the command log as debug messages by `set -s` as this command does not send the commands to the command log. This feature is disabled by default.

## Decision: Introduce `DataPlane` objects, so the `context` and `db` structures
effectively no longer exist.
Given two `DataPlane` instances in practice, we can:
(1) generate a set of unique tuples on a given time index and
	"spread" the data they contain into an `(e, a, v)` tuple.
(2) treat the entire `DataPlane` as a table and each of the `e`, `a`
	and `v` columns as if they were separate tables (i.e. all
	their arrangements have the same "column name").
The `DataPlane` instance will keep its own internal copy of the
structure of all arrangements which have been seen and can effectively
make those copies available to any `Db` or `ImplContext`.

The instances are not fully generic (no self-referential tuples), but
that is a requirement of our index for Datomic.

Each data plane can have its own index struct, in order to be as
flexible as possible. 

Each `DataPlane::get_column` returns a nested `Vec<Value>` which
may be thought of as a single time index for that field. 

The current `impl_id` of an `EnsembleInstance` remains its
"primary key" or tuple id.

The new approach will, in most cases, require a second pass over the
dataset, and a new "projection" of the data.

## Decision: In this case, the state of an aggregate is that of its processes, which
should be used to modify the state associated with the domain itself.

In the case of a process, this is done by passing all the state required for its
functionality into the process, and only returning when the process has been
completed. So in this case the state is provided to the process explicitly.

In the case of an aggregate that has no state, its state is explicitly provided
when the aggregate is instantiated, and its process is only activated when the
aggregate has been instantiated. In this case, it is up to the implementation
to decide the proper meaning of "state".

For the sake of clarity and simplicity, we will in this case only address the
case of events that are state-less, with all other state being provided by other
means. In the case of a state-less event, the "state" is provided by a key/value
pair where the key is the state, and the value is everything else.

However, a state-less event may also be used to return a new state. This would
usually be a "before" type of event that takes a state into account but returns
a new state that removes that state.

## Decision: ### Client's response to the error:

We've decided to use the client's HTTP `Status*` response header, rather than custom errors, because:

- It is part of the HTTP protocol.
- It indicates all information required by the API to validate the request.
- It's not required for success.

To do this we will require some additional information in case of invalid requests. A request that can be marked as 4XX
has to provide an ID. This ID should be marked with a `X-Content-Type` header with a value of `application/json`.
Requests marked with a `X-Content-Type` header cannot be routed. So if the `ID` is missing, there's no way of
tracing the request through the network and we will send an error while processing it.

Example:

```http
PUT http://api.example.com/user/1234
Content-Type: application/json
X-Content-Type: application/json
User-Id: 1234
X-User-Id: 1234

...

200 OK
...
```

If a request is marked with a `X-Content-Type` header, it would be ideal to send a response code of 204 (No Content)
for a successful request. Additionally, when using the `content-type` header as described above, a request code
of 400 Bad Request should be sufficient.

However, we're currently using middleware that will always send some information back, whether or not there was an error.
Additionally, the middleware only expects a single information header. 

Our middleware will be removed. Requests that are marked with a `X-Content-Type` header, will use the `Body`
instead as the error code (or part of it), as requested above.

### The Server's response to the error:

Server-side errors should be explicitly marked as such in JSON responses, as described in [Server Error
Messages](#server-error-messages).

The case of the datatset being isolated from its versions is a tricky one.
It implies a dataset which is set up before any version.

## Decision: * Should be easy to store schema definitions
* Should be easy to version/control schemas (for multiple environments)
* Should be easy to deploy and migrate
* Should provide access to relevant schema elements (tables, views, stored procedures, etc)
* 
### Key Definitions

These terms should be common across all environments:
- **Database Schema**: All the tables, views, and other objects used by a particular application and in an envirnoment.

- **Database Version**: The version number of the actual DB (not the schema.) 

- **Schema Version**: The version number of the schema (tables, views, stored procedures, etc.)

- **Schema Registry**: The place where schemas are stored. 
(In this instance, we have decided that the schema registry is the Git repository).

- **Schema Definition**: In the context of the Git repository, the definition is a set of SQL statements (CREATE and drop syntax) used by a migration to change the DB Schema.

### Considerations on DB Environment (env)

- The "env" should be an artifact/annotation of our infrastructure.
- 1 env per organization. 
- Can (but not has to) be the same as the deployment. 
    * Ex. If we had a Dev, Test, and Production env in Git, and we deployed to three different servers, our deployment would be three envs in total.
- 
### Schemas are versioned, and each version of a schema defines a migration path from the prior version of the DB. 

- Migration files live in the "migration" dir under a source tree.
    * The migration path defined by a migration file applies to a particular deployment of the database, given its version.
- 
### Migration syntax:
(All CREATE statements can be rolled back, and should)
```sql
CREATE TABLE my_table (
    column1 VARCHAR(255),
    column2 VARCHAR(255),
    ...
);
```
- Drop statements should be in comments (so they're rolled back automatically)
- In most cases, we will roll our own migrations, so we will only use a schema registry if it's beneficial to do so.
- 
### How we store the schemas:
- We will store each Schema Definition in a subdirectory in our Git.

## Decision: Previously the Value column was present since the previous engine (for the value) was not a JDBC column. However as mentioned above
using the "true" column is less intuitive and more an engine need.

For the same purpose we use the "raw", "unparsed", "native" and "binary" (in all cases - binary refers to binary encoded value)
fields.

These fields provide the data from the binary value as-is.
This is meant for cases when the user expects a "binary" value (e.g. image in an image pipeline).
There can be just binary value at a particular index, however, most of the times there are other columns for a binary value.
For example, if there is binary data, the engine will first extract the "binary" column and then the values as binary bytes.

Example:

Key: | Value: <image> | [binary=false] | [binary=true] | [binary=false] | [binary=false] | [binary=false] |
Value: |[image][binary=false] | -1 | 1 | -1 | -1 | -1 |

- - is used to represent the binary encoding type.
- 0 indicates binary value present, 1 indicates it is a binary value binary encoded, and 0 indicates it is a normal value.

The engine is expected to be "binary encoded" at a particular index from its point of view for binary encoding.
All the elements are signed and are interpreted as bytes.

## Decision: We will adopt a process of collaborative architectural decision-making that
exposes each proposal to broad review within the development team and provides
a mechanism for all stakeholders to weigh in.

The process entails the following steps:

1.  A community member creates a pull request (PR) on [GitHub][pull-request],
    detailing an alternative to the current behavior or functionality. The PR should
    be as specific as possible and articulate the reasons for change. The PR should
    be accompanied by (or reference) an Architectural Decision Record, documenting
    the context and rationale for the proposal.

1.  The PR is held until all reviewers have weighed in.

1.  After a period of time (1 week), a community-wide vote is held on [Discord]
    in the relevant channel, polling all Discord members for their opinions.

1.  All data from all sources (PRs, Discord votes, community discussion, etc.) is
    collected and presented to the core developers and TSC in a shared document.

1.  The core developers and TSC discuss the proposal, taking into consideration all
    available information.

1.  The core developers and TSC vote on the proposal, using the same voting
    process as the community vote.

1.  After the vote, all community members are invited to review the vote results and
    to discuss the outcome.

1.  The core developers and TSC may choose to
    [reconsider](https://github.com/npryce/office-scripts/commit/507673577547875567676997c737b27543c68687#diff-507673577547875567676997c737b27543c68687-53309772851677758924913436061602588351276590324713498162077529730224271088775265468658795

## Decision: These aspects of GreenLog are handled by Handlers. They handle log entries *before* they reach the rest of GreenLog.

### Handlers as context inducers
GreenLog's context system has two "levels". Context is added at middleware level, and at record level.
The middleware context is available to all records, and may be manipulated by handlers to tailor records' output (e.g. the formatter or handler will be asked to tailor the format string with values present in their context).
In order to preserve context throughout the chain of processing, we add context at the record level.

Handlers are supplied with a `Context` object of their own at the beginning of their execution. This allows them to manipulate (e.g. add) additional context, to filter entries from their "feed", or add attributes or other details to each entry. This can happen _before_ the entry is supplied to the rest of GreenLog.
### Handlers as in-memory buffers
There is no natural in-memory "handling" of log entries.
To maintain a buffer of log entries in-memory, a GreenLog handler must be able to communicate with its own memory. This is by definition a different state from the environment, in the form of a "local" state.
This local state is handled by a dedicated component (GreenLog), so that the handler is able to communicate with this local state.

## Decision: This is an [issue](https://github.com/publishing-apps/rummager/issues/16) that will be resolved
by adding a new publishing task to the publishing API that reads `message` content and
event data from the messaging system, triggers a Sidekiq task and then marks the publishing
event as done. The Sidekiq worker takes care of performing the required work on the
message by calling the `index_published_data` function on the data object.

This approach splits the responsibility for handling message retries between the message
handler and the publishing data object. The message handler knows nothing about
retries or failures, and has no control over the underlying behaviour. This removes knowledge
of the retries or failure conditions from the publishing API.

The message handler also removes dependencies from the publishing API and simplifies the code that
is used to register the publishing event. A new publishing event is defined by the
`message` field. The data is deserialised from the message by the message handler.

This changes the flow from:

### current

The publishing API marks the `message` as processed by pushing it into the queue `RummapperReadStream`.
The `RummapperReadStream` marks the message as read by calling the `MessageBrokerReadStream.mark_message_as_read`,
the message handler marks the message as done by calling `PublishingData.create_sidekiq_task`.

### new

The message handler reads the message and the metadata, and marks the publishing event as done
by triggering the Sidekiq task, which uses the `index_published_data` method on the
data object to perform the required work. The message handler is removed from the publishing API
message chain.

A new publishing event is defined by the `message` field. The data is deserialised from the
message by the message handler.

There are several advantages of this approach:

* Separation of concerns
* `mark_message_as_read` still applies at publishing app level
* Enables a more lightweight implementation of publish events, by decoupling from the details of
  how the message is deserialised or communicated.
* Additional error handling can be added between the triggering of the Sidekiq task and the
  `index_published_data` call.

## Decision: Dialect self-encoding is treated as distinct from the rest of the document. If a node does not belong to dialect "self-encoded", 
we do not render it. 

Any JSON-LD node belongs to exactly one dialect, either dialect "self-encoded" or dialect "flattened".

We will render both Dialect prefixes and the Dialect URL in the document.
Both are a reference to the same dialect. 
We'll put `/@` before the dialect URL.

For instance, given a Dialect:

```json
{
  "@type": "Dialect",
  "name": "example-dialect",
  "short": "exd",
  "id": "http://example.org/exd",
  "prefixes": {
    "exd": "http://example.org/exd"
  },
  "main_node_id": "#example"
}
```

And a Dialect self-encoding:

```json
{
  "type": "Dialect",
  "name": "example-dialect",
  "short": "exd",
  "id": "http://example.org/exd",
  "prefixes": {
    "exd": "http://example.org/exd"
  },
  "main_node_id": "#example"
}
``` 

That self-encoding will be transformed as a dialect domain element by adding an "@" symbol between the @type and id fields.
The resulting dialect domain element will be:

```json
{
  "type": "Dialect",
  "name": "example-dialect",
  "short": "exd",
  "id": "http://example.org/exd",
  "prefixes": {
    "exd": "http://example.org/exd"
  },
  "main_node_id": "#example"
}
```

* `name` can be mutable within a transaction, whereas `id` cannot be changed (see above)
* `name` should reflect a natural key property of the entity.
* `name` should be consistent with what is stored in the local representation of the entity. For example, IDs should only be used as part of the name when creating a new entity.
* `id` fields should be formed using a standardized naming convention per domain (e.g. UUID).
* use a consistent encoding of all ID fields
* new domains should be able to support `name` in addition to `id` fields (e.g. GitHub commit ids support both)
* new domains should not have to support mutations or cascading effects of rename operations

## Decision: We will use the trusted CA. We will not use any kind of certificate pinning.

### Host-level

This is done as a host level process (client or server process, either as a dependency or part of the runtime) - there are numerous libraries depending on the language/platform. Here, we have relied on the operating system:

- Debian: (See /etc/ssl/certs - managed by `openssl` by default)
- Ubuntu: (See /etc/ssl/certs - managed by `openssl` by default)
- Arch Linux: (See /etc/ssl/certs - managed by `openssl` by default)
- CentOS: (See /etc/ssl/certs - managed by `openssl` by default)
- Fedora: (See /etc/ssl/certs - managed by `openssl` by default)
- ...

You can be assured that using unverified certificates with this default setup would degrade to a "bad," "unknown," and "untrusted" certificate. Using a trusted CA will keep an already trusted certificate in the server, and the trust will extend to the rest of the Public Key.

### TLS/SSL-level

Here, we are relying on the implementation of the language/runtime. Different libraries have their own methods of certificate verification. Different architectures are implemented. For most cases, the implementation is similar enough to be called a trust.

- OpenSSL: (See /root/ssl - managed by openssl_config_source.in by default)
- gnutls: (See /lib/gnutls - managed by gnutls_config_source.in by default)
- OpenBizSSL: (See /lib/openszllib - managed by openszlib_config_source.in by default)
- ...

### Dependencies

Every application we've written has its own dependencies and their respective OpenSSL installations in their own unique places. However, because gnutls also provides a OpenSSL library, and also because gnutls_config_source.in typically relies on OpenSSL to begin with, we can make the most of that (see in gnutls_config_source.in and -Wall option).

## Decision: We decided to go with "openHAB core" approach for the moment since we want to be able to have "base" and "complete" runtime.
"Complete" runtime will depend on "base" runtime, which provides all the necessary features to initialize the "complete" runtime.
This is exactly the desired behavior since all the features from the "base" runtime should be available in the "complete" runtime.
That would imply that all the dependencies from the "base" runtime are required in "complete" runtime.

Now to fix the compile time issue, we decided to split the "base" and "complete" runtime into separate modules.
Dependencies of a feature should be defined in the "base" runtime module.
For example, `openhab-core-base` module would depend on `org.eclipse.OSGi`, `org.eclipse.core`, `org.eclipse.event`, etc.
These dependencies are common for most of the openHAB core features.
Modules of the "complete" runtime will depend on the "base" runtime.
Example, the "complete" runtime may have modules `org.eclipse.winery`, `org.eclipse.jetty`, `org.eclipse.jetty-management`, etc.
Most of those modules are unnecessary because they are common for most of the openHAB runtime features.
This approach does not fully resolve the problem because those dependencies are still accessible for plugins and features (for instance) without any mechanism for controlling access to those packages.
But as we cannot really force plugins and features to only depend on dependencies that are required for them,
we think that this will be best possible solution for solving compile time dependencies issue.
Any dependencies between modules should be put into a "complete" runtime module.

In addition to fixing compile time errors and allowing for easier development of new features,
this structure of splitting core into "base" and "complete" runtime simplifies potential "upgrades" and "migrations" from "base" to "complete" runtime.
All that is needed for such an upgrade is to update the references of modules and to remove the base runtime dependency on any feature in the complete runtime.
Example:
```
[openhab thing core] <--- [openhab rest core]
|                                             |
|-----------------------------------------------|
|           new "complete" runtime             |
|-----------------------------------------------|
|

## Decision: The URIs are the base name of the resource as defined in the W3C Resource Description Framework. These are constructed with required parts (the base name), optional extension parts.

* A URI can be constructed from one or more base names.
* A URI can have zero or many extension parts.
* In this implementation (RDA), URI construction results in a string that starts with a base name and optionally follows it with zero or many extension parts.
* URIS use the `@` symbol as the URI suffix in a name of an ordered sequence.
* URIS may optionally use a `.` symbol in the base name to distinguish labels from metadata.
* The URI concatenation mechanism is string concatenation.
* The component separation symbol is the `@` symbol.
* URIS must be no longer than 32 characters when encoded using UTF-8 or ISO-8601, using the length of the base name as the first component and one byte after that for each extension part.
* Extensions parts use the `@` symbol.
* Extension part length must be non-negative.
* URIS are case-sensitive.
* If a URI consists of base name and extension part, the last part is a non-empty sequence of one or more bytes that contains only of the characters `%`, `/`, `:`, ‘@’ and ‘-’ (`-` is for `-` to be represented in the URI).
* A URI is valid only if it follows all the rules for syntax.
* A URI must be unique within its domain, as to avoid conflicts or naming collisions.

**Example**

```
uri:http://www.example.com/book
uri:http://www.example.com/book/chapter
uri:http://www.example.com/book/chapter/section
uri:http://www.example.com/article
uri:http://www.example.com/projects/Kubuntu-PIM34/Kubuntu-PIM34%29-Release%20Package#
uri:http://www.example.com/projects/Kubuntu-PIM34/Kubuntu-PIM34%29-Release%20Package#%29-Package

## Decision: Allow HTTP calls to ORCID to be made only by authorised applications.

We will use token authentication for this. Each application will have a token.

Token authentication is implemented via [Auth0](https://auth0.com/docs/connect/token-authentication/) which is an Auth0 app designed to make token authentication easy and secure.

Requests from non-authorised applications will be rejected.

It is important to keep the information in the token secret (i.e. not visible to others). Therefore we cannot store the data in a public repository.
This means that we should make sure that the token stays secret even when deployed. 

The current consensus is that this is done by not including the data in version control, i.e. not in any `config.toml` file in the codebase.

The token should be stored at the application level in a file such as `config.toml`, or in an environment variable. This is because applications often need to configure other settings.

Each environment will have a corresponding token. We need different tokens for environment (development, production) as they often have different uses.

### Architecture

![Structure of application, token and API client](diagram.png)

- The application will be configured to contain a token.
- The token will be stored in the configuration.
- The API client will be configured with a token.
- A local [ORCID OAuth2 Token Client](https://github.com/LBHackney-IT/orcdatadictionary/tree/feature/orcid2019-1/applications/orcidOAuth2TokenClient) is used to sign the requests (as documented in its [README](https://github.com/LBHackney-IT/orcdatadictionary/tree/feature/orcid2019-1/applications/orcidOAuth2TokenClient/README.md)).
- You will need a local development environment (i.e. a machine in which to make development locally).
- You should keep all the information in the `config.toml` secure.

### Example

```toml
[orcdatadictionary]
token = "aaaa8765-654321"
```

## Decision: Proxy configuration via environment variable used by non-Docker client applications (i.e. `curl`, `wget`, python, javascript, or any other program other than docker itself).
- Proxy configuration via environment variable will be handled as follows:
  - `-f`, `--force`, `-s`, and `-v` options to be ignored
  - `-L`, `--login`, and `-U` (non-lowercase versions) should be treated as non-existent
  - `-K` or `--key` will be treated as a file path
- Proxy configuration as environment variables should use lowercase names and "http" or "https" prefixes as in the environment variable names for each application.
  - `http_proxy`, `https_proxy` and `http_proxy_pass`
- Proxy configurations for the hostnames of the proxies should use the DNS name (name of the server as a hostname, e.g. `http://www.example.com`) of the proxy host.
- A `no_proxy` value can be provided by the environment.
  - Will use DNS resolution
  - Will ignore the `no_proxy` value of non-Docker client applications.
  - `NO_PROXY` environment variable: Will use DNS resolution
  - `no_proxy_all` and `no_proxy_main` values cannot be ignored by any system.
- An environment variable can be set to null, empty, or a string
  - `-v` option should be required
  - `-s` option should be required
  - `-f` option should be required
  - `-L` option should be required
- If the `no_proxy` is set when the system uses an environment proxy, the connection will fail, and `curl`, `wget`, r, etc. will be terminated.
- `-K` environment variables should be prefixed with `K:` to ensure that no subsequent environment variables are configured using the same name.
- `-U` environment variables should be used to set a User-Agent string.

The purpose of proxy configuration using environment variables is to support non-Docker clients.
  - When a Docker client is used, proxy configuration is ignored.
  - Docker should be run in "proxy" mode by using the `-s` option.
  - `-s` option implies `-f` and `-L`

- `n = 1` - Double-signing block number cannot be checked

  - A validator should be considered "voting in the new-votes vote" if (1) it is on the voting set of a block AND (2) the timestamp of the voting key is after the first half of the block height.

## Decision: The Wikibase release number will consist of all the digits prior to the '.'. The first digit will be the minor release number for the Wikibase release (version 0,1 or 2), the last digit will be the patch number for the Wikibase release (the current patch number for the Wikibase release).

### Wikibase patch release procedure:

- A new Wikibase version is cut and tagged with `WMBX-1`, which is equivalent to `1.0.0` (minor = 0 and patch = 0)
- Release candidates for the Wikibase version will be tagged with `WMBX-2`, which is equivalent to `1.0.1` (minor = 0 and patch = 1)
- Minor and patch releases of the Wikibase version will be tagged with `WMBX-3`, which is equivalent to `1.0.2` (minor = 0 and patch = 2)
- WMF will publish a patch release of MediaWiki which would contain the fix (or bug). An example of these tags are the releases tagged by WMF as `mediawiki-1.36.0-2`.
- A new patch release is cut for the Wikibase version and tagged with `WMBX-4`, which is equivalent to `1.0.3` (minor = 0 and patch = 3)
- With the purpose of creating a new version of the Wikibase release that comes with the fixes as described above a new tag name will be used:
    - The release number of the Wikibase version can be taken from the previous release number (`WMBX-002`, which is equivalent to `1.0.2`) and incremented by `1`, resulting in `WMBX-003`
    - A new tag will be created and use the previous release number concatenated with the string `-RC` and then incremented by `1`:
        - `wmbx-002-RC` will be a release candidate for a patch release, with an equivalent tag as `WMBX-003`
        - `wmbx-003-RC` will be a release candidate for a minor release, with an equivalent tag as `WMBX-004`

## Decision: We've chosen to not follow a merge-before-deploy practice for ArgoCD Application's, and by extension, ArgoCD itself.

While we could, there's nothing to truly benefit us for taking this approach. 

One reason for this is that it is a single instance deployment system, meaning applications are only available when the ArgoCD nodes are active. This means that those apps would only be deployed when ArgoCD is applied - which in turn means that the apps will only live so long as the ArgoCD is up and running, even if those apps are merged in, etc.

In any case, we would have to get an appropriate URL to the ArgoCD applications repo, and then we'd do the following:

1. create an internal repo for the ArgoCD applications (called `--applications` in this repo that we are currently using)
1. configure ArgoCD in our environment to use the `--applications` repo with a url
1. ensure that ArgoCD has a "high" priority or `pre-install`
1. set ArgoCD to deploy "all" apps on each deployment, such that `AppManifestMerge` will always apply those applications no matter what.

This is a risky process and not necessary - because ArgoCD is configured as an *instance* (not cluster-wide) deployment, we can get them available simply by getting their URL, and setting ArgoCD to deploy all applications on each deployment.

## Decision: * The versioning for the client will be by the group name. The versioning strategy for the client depends on whether the target API has a version number or not.
  * In order to do that we need a version number for the client to be able to compare it to the version of the entity which the client is attempting to communicate with. 
  * There are a number of client groups in use. Different groups might not necessarily be able to communicate using the same API
  * There can exist multiple client groups, for example `d320d8-12-0` and `d320d8-12-1`. These two groups require the same API client as the same version.
* *If there is no version available for the client, then the version of the service will have to be used.

### Semantic Versioning

The version is split in two parts `minor`, `patch`.
- `major` version increment is made when an incompatible change is made, for example:
  - deprecations are added to an API
  - a public method is renamed
  - a public method is deprecated
  - a class is moved or deleted
  - a package name is changed
  - a set of files (e.g. an API definition) is moved
- `minor` version increment is made when a compatible change is made, for example:
  - a public method is added to the API
  - a type is added to the API
  - a class is added to the API
  - a field is added to a type
  - a field is moved within a type
- `patch` version increment is made when a incompatible change is made to an existing type/class/field (see above).
- Example: incrementing the version when moving an implementation
  ```
  from v4.4.0 to v4.5.0 there can be some patch-like change, such as:
  Move implementation from a place and bring it to the service. 
  Increment minor version to v4.4.1, v4.3.0
  ```

### Other groups

Other groups are `d870c0-0` and `d870c0-1`, with `-1` being the equivalent of `d870c0`.

## Decision: In abstract terms, every resource node has two states (state of existence) and a lifecycle.

### The Lifecycle
The lifecycle starts with the creation and ends at the destruction. Therefore, a resource lifecycle happens at all phases - archival and all other phases.

### The Lifecycle Phases
Every lifecycle has several phases. The phases are named after state-transitions that a resource is going through. We can identify the phases as follows:
- An _Initial State_ - where the resource enters into the workflow.
- Phase 1 - this phase is a beginning of the active phase (a lifecycle phase)
- Phase 2 - the phase of resource state transition
- Phase 3 - the phase of resource state transition
- `End State` - that is an ultimate state of our resource lifecycle. 

#### Actions in the phases
Each phase should be as fast as possible, as it concerns only the temporal phase of the resource state transition. In the sense of _action_ in the context of the phases it refers to a time period. 
Every active lifecycle phase should be followed by an `End State`. The `End State` can be the same as the `Initial State` or it can be different - it doesn't matter. We just need to ensure, that a resource lifecycle has a beginning and an end.

The above description is valid for both processes and queues, as those are two main types of resources (both are encapsulated in the same `Resource` class).

## Decision: The design specifies a system with a single global registry of modules and services, that has the following properties:

- **Autonomy**: the system can be run as an isolated application, where its registry contains only the modules relevant to it.
- **Configuration**: the system allows any user or module to specify their own set of modules via configuration settings.
- **Customizable startup order**: The system allows the startup of a module or service to be dependent on a specified set of other modules, with the dependencies listed in a set.
- **Dependency satisfaction**: When modules depend on each other, the dependent modules will be started after their dependencies.
- **No runtime changes to configuration**: All user-defined configuration settings should be set *before* the startup phase.
- **Configuration stored in source control**: Configuration should be stored under version control as part of the module/application code.
- **Modules allowed to depend on eachother**: Modules can specify other modules as dependencies using standard convention.
- **Modules not allowed to depend on runtime data**: Modules cannot reference a set of modules available in runtime at startup. This rule prevents a module from depending on data about the system in which it is running.

## Decision: When we believe we have one less component than fluxes,
and we are unable to resolve the system using priors,
then we have an underdetermined system.
Given an underdetermined system,
we believe that each of the unknowns can be resolved
from the measurements and prior information.
However, we also believe that the system
should be resolved as though the additional
unknowns are constraints with prior distributions
that are centered on a known value.
In most of these cases, this means that
the priors for these unknowns should be centered
on zero.

Generally, there are three possibilities when performing
underdetermined calculations:
(1) We believe that we have a prior.
For an unknown with one degree of freedom,
our prior should be centered on a "known" value.
A prior for an unknown with multiple degrees of freedom
should be centered on the prior mean distribution.
(2) We do not know what the prior distribution is,
and we think each unknown
has multiple degrees of freedom,
yet we cannot accurately determine each of the prior distributions.
In this case, we think that the prior distributions
should be centered on one another.
(3) We do not know the prior distribution of the unknown,
and it's likely that it has many degrees of freedom.
We're unable to determine their relative distributions
in this case as well.
Additionally, we can't even know when a
system will be underdetermined.

## Decision: * UI should notify if setting a component in the wrong state that is prevented from running
* This can also effectively halt a reconnection attempt.
* The setting to prevent the deadlock should be set at the instance and/or group configuration level, or even better, be a plugin property.

### Option 1
* We could modify the UI process to be able to request a restart without synchronizing the state transitions.
* To this end we would need information about the current phases of Interlok components to be able to perform the request properly.
* Given Interlok cannot currently communicate via the DAL to the running instance, we may have to use interlok configuration, such as the `instance_info` and `instance_config` configuration properties to store all our information to attempt a `restart`
* This information could even be hard coded.
* By using a `restart` request which is not synchronized, the UI should be able to continue where it's left off rather than getting stuck.
* If the UI is using asynchronous, synchronous or wait settings (or options), we should set them appropriately when sending the `restart` request.
* We would then need to send the actual `restart` request via `request()`, then `applyConfiguration` and `commitConfiguration`.
* Finally we would be using the `restart` function as `getCommand()`.
* A problem here, of course, is that any request to a component must check that the component is not in the wrong state, and the reset state will be dependent on the state.
* That is, the UI process, which likely a different process, likely doesn't hold all the required configurations, and is forced to query the Interlok instance.

## Decision: GraphQL it is. GraphQL query language is beautiful and powerful. We don't need to overengineer things.

GraphQL also allows clients to get everything they need in one request (as opposed to many other APIs that force you to get back more than you need).

GraphQL is great for small teams or individuals. If we scale up to multiple services it will be more work to maintain, but the clients will be able to more easily scale with our services.

GraphQL can be implemented on the server side without extra tooling. The tool we'll use already implements GraphQL (Popster), so it's easy to adopt.

GraphQL can be slow, if we have many tables in the datastore or have multiple services each using their own query language. The query layer is slow and expensive.

But all our APIs have some kind of query layer; in the case of REST APIs, that is HTTP. A GraphQL query language is a natural evolution of HTTP, so it's appropriate for this context.

We're already familiar with GraphQL as it's used in some of our services (ArgoCD).

## Decision: We will create two integer fields:

- The `code` of a transaction: This field is encoded with 100,000,000
  consecutive bits (100% of our current memory), with the "error code" bits
  in the high-order bits (eg. `255` is an invalid type, `254` is an error, etc.).
  We will call this field the `result` field because it only contains
  messages for "successful" (0) or "failed" (1) operations.

- The `error_code` of a transaction: This field is encoded in 64 bits. We
  will call this the `code_error` field because the number of bits can grow
  on us. Therefore, we can't map every 64-bit code to a particular error
  string and, although we can make a long enumeration of errors for each
  possible error_code (eg. 0x00000001 = `InvalidTransaction`), in most
  cases (over the 64-bit space), we will have to use a
  [custom encoding](https://github.com/tendermint/abci/issues/221)
  for the client to decode. We have suggested three options:
    1. 3-byte encoding of the most significant bits of the error code, where
        `0` is `ok` and all other values are errors. `1` means something
        more specific than just `ok`, where the number of bits depends
        on the specific error
    2. We could also encode the error code as a double-byte. This could be
        easier for some clients as we can use the most significant bits of
        the error code to form a range of "error types", where values will
        map to certain kinds of errors and can be used for error handling
    3. Another possibility would be using the least significant bits for
        a set of predefined errors. We can call these "known" errors and
        "custom" errors.

## Decision: We should switch the `BodyBlock` model to a `Block` model instead. We've already done most of the work for liveblog rendering
using post-production scripts (see PR#982). Post-production will still use the current model, but we have the building blocks
to be able to switch to a new model as soon as the new post-production code is able to be moved into production.

### CAPI Block Elements in the Post-Production Model

Currently, the only element type that lives in the `BodyBlock` post-production model is `Text`, which can come in 
its 5 forms - paragraph, list item, bold, italics, underline.

### CAPI Block Elements in the Post-Production Model

As the new post-production model is `Block` and each `Block` represents an unordered list of block elements that live within it:
here are the descriptions of the elements in the new model.

- **Block:** a single block element
    - **Text:** 
        - **Paragraph:** several lines of text, usually one or more paragraphs
        - **List Item:** a single line of text, with an associated bullet or list number
        - **Bold:** text with the words bolded
        - **Italics:** text with the words italicized
        - **Underline:** text with the words underlined
- **Block:** any of the elements listed above
- **BlockElement:** an element

### CAPI Block Elements in the Post-Production Model (Summary)

Our `BodyBlock` post-production model will consist of:

- `Blocks`: the list of block elements
    - `Text`: the text of the paragraph, lists, bold, italics, underline
        - `Paragraph`: several lines of text
        - `List Item`: a single line of text, with a bullet or number
        - `Bold`: paragraph, list item, or other elements with bolded text
        - `Italics`: paragraph, list item, or other elements with italicized text
        - `Underline`: paragraph, list item, or other elements with underlined text
- `Blocks`: all the elements in the block
    - `Block`: a single block element
        - `Text`: the text of paragraph, list item, bold, italics, underline
            - `Paragraph`: several lines

The middleware should add an extra HTTP header, `Authorization: Bearer $token` when it is executed.

## Decision: ### Chosen Candidate: Format files programmatically

This candidate makes it as easy as possible for a developer to ensure files are formatted in a consistent way.

Because each developer has a single responsibility for ensuring files are correctly formatted, a programmatic approach is the best way of balancing developer convenience with quality control.

Running format files is not a "developer convenience", but instead an extra step that guards against inconsistency. Because this is not part of a developer's workflow, it's okay to view it as a bonus.

This is also the only solution that makes it as easy as possible for a build pipeline or CI tool to ensure files are correctly formatted. Building consistently requires the CI tool or build pipeline to know what the expected formatting is, and automatically running the formatting program ensures this is known.

The specific run command used to run the format file is documented [here](0004-choose-tool-for-formatting-files.md).

    `Program.set_program_data`, so that that all the instructions, by the end of the program, call `Program.exit_program()`. However we do that, we would have to be careful not to forget any specific instruction.
2. We can add our own conventions to avoid such cases, or we can add helpers with patterns that cover the most common cases. That can be solved by the language that is implemented in the processor, and therefore, we can only add those conventions to our tools, and not to the language itself, or to the processor architecture.

A real example of this can be seen in the `program_example.c`, where there is a loop, that is executed until the last instruction. Instead of having a `break` or `return` before the loop, the program would be updated so that after the loop, there is a call to `Program.exit_program()`.

## Decision: After reviewing how we bulk load data in Rummager's search indexes and seeing some of the issues that were still present and some of the additional issues that were created, we decided that the best method for bulk loading popularity
data for the search indexes is by performing an in place popularity update during the bulk operation, rather than as a separate operation.
By doing this:

1. Popularity updates can happen asynchronously as an integration task in publishing.
2. A rummager process using the publishing API and bulk delete can be created with a specific command that is triggered using a nightly job
3. The publishing API will handle the message from the NightlyJob.

### Advantages of this method

1. Popularity updates occur asynchronously. This is beneficial when a message is consumed from the publishing API as the load process is only triggered once nightly, and the specific time it arrives is unknown.
1. This is in line with our bulk update, using the publishing API for the data and, therefore, the metadata.
1. Popularity data is written on every message, including a timestamp of when the record was inserted.

### Limitations of this method

1. We cannot search based upon popularity updates done on a document since the field is updated in the publishing API in a non-deterministic way.

1. Search results are affected in a non-deterministic way by an integration job.
1. No performance guarantee can be given since it is dependent on the behavior of the publishing API and rummager.
1. Nightly Jobs are not able to enforce time constraints - so there is no guarantee that the popularity update will occur within a specific time.

## Decision: [Volley](http://www.VolleyProject.org/) is an alternative HTTP client, that suffers from a different problem: it only supports `GET` requests. Volley is very comprehensive and has various options to set the request headers: `Content-Type`, `Accept`, `Authorization`, etc. 

Moreover, we need to think of the return codes. The API can return HTTP `4XX` or `5XX` errors. JAX-RS guarantees that the response body contains a JSON with a `message` field, providing a reasonable generic description of the error. The HTTP status code, while also meaningful, will be the minimum amount of information that can be reported as a result of the request.

Volley has a response mode that is somewhat equivalent to the `ResponseBody` mode of other HTTP clients. It sets a byte array, which is then used as is for the client's request. This allows us to treat the error response and the successful response of an API endpoint as the same type, an `HTTP Response` class or something similar, which contains the status code, the response headers, the response body and possibly other information.

## Decision: Change the default date format to `yyyy/mm/dd` (ISO 8601).

Provide scripts to enable converting existing `dd/mm/yyyy` dates to ISO format.
Also known as `dateformat`, `strftime`, or `date-template`.
It is available in most languages including Javascript, Python, and Go.

A new `config.sh` variable `ADR_DATE` will be provided to define the input
format instead of overriding the entire date format.  This enables a more
fine-grained control over the input format of dates.

For example, `config.sh` might include:
```
ADR_DATE=$(date +%y%m%d)
```
or
```
ADR_DATE=$(date -I -s "2017-08-09")
```
The above examples use the builtin Unix date functions.

If `ADR_DATE` is specified, `ADR_DATE` should be used when format dates.

An example of the difference in formatting provided in a log message:
```
The date and time are: `08/09/2017` 
```
becomes
```
The date and time are: `2017-08-09`
```
Using the same value of `ADR_DATE`.

## Decision: Add the feature to block specific sprout nodes with the maximum number of retries allowed for each direction. 
A sprout node, receiving block requests, must set the `request-id` parameter in each request in the same 
direction and block the corresponding request in the `failed` field if `numberOfRetries` of block number 
is exceeded. 
The P-CSCF can set the sprout nodes' configurations for block and timeout by using the features of the
`request-id`, as described in the `RequestHeaders` parameter.

Sprout nodes should block `failed` requests after `numberOfRetries` times, for both incoming and outgoing
requests. 
If all requests of a direction are failed and `numberOfRetries` is exceeded, then all unfailed requests in the 
corresponding direction should be cancelled.

## Decision: We divide the James features and artifacts into **four levels**. The levels define the boundaries between
user and vendor responsibility. 

[A feature] of a James mail server can be [classified] into one of the following levels
based on its [inherent risk](1): 

* **Level 1 (Feature).** An optional feature that requires the user to make an explicit decision
to opt in. **Risk:** low.
* **Level 2 (Feature).** Optional features that need opt in, but which have more 
risk than level 1 features. **Risk:** medium.
* **Level 3 (Feature).** Optional features that do not require opt in. **Risk:** high.
* **Level 4 (Feature).** Mandatory features. **Risk:** null.

| | Level 1 (Feature) | Level 2 (Feature) | Level 3 (Feature) | Level 4 (Feature) |
|-------|---------|-----|---------|----|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|--- |--- |--- |
| Risk | [low] | [high] | [low] | [low] | [high] | [low] | [low] | [low] | [low] | - | - | - |
| Description | Optional | Optional | Optional | Mandatory | | | | | | | - | - | - |

1. All the above risk levels refer to the risk of not working out-of-the-box and/or causing confusion in the daily lives of users (configuration, maintenance, etc).
	
The above-listed components are not only artifacts, but are also *features*. A feature can be optional.
If such a feature does not opt-in, then it is "mandatory" by default.

## Decision: An additional piece of context is that all of these changes will be part of a migration that will be split into a few increments. We expect to be able to take advantage of a rollback mechanism for each stage of the migration, if any of them fail in particular. 

### Versioning

Our versioning model in this codebase has the following meaning:

- **M** is the stage of our data model for the code in a particular branch.
- **A** is the stage of our architecture for the code in a branch.
- **D** is the stage of our deployment configuration.
- **V** is the stage of our data migration of all the data.

The data migration is all the way back to `v0` of our implementation and will be rolled back in the event that any stage of the migration fails. The schema is updated in a controlled way and backwards compatibility is maintained where possible.

### Commit

Each commit must be backed by one or more of the following descriptions:

- **[migration](0012-migrate-to-graphql.md)** - all the commits in this branch are part of a data migration from a previous version of the code (a release)
- **[architecture](0011-change-persistence-mechanism.md)** - all the commits in this branch are related to an architectural change

## Decision: We’ve decided to transform our external `elements` into a new data type called `Transformable`, which is basically a regular mapping of `domain` -> `internal`. 

```javascript
const externalElements = [
    [
        { externalDomain: 1 },
        { externalDomain: 2 },
    ],
    [
        { externalDomain: 3 },
        { externalDomain: 4 },
    ],
];
```

In this new mapping, `domain` has its actual value, and `internal` contains the internal representation of that domain within our model, as a transformable type.

So as a result, `internal` is transformed out of the `externalDomain` of the transformed elements.

This solution requires:

- users to transform each domain into a transformable with the correct mapping
- all consumers of our model to include the transformation both by including it in their `lib-prosemirror-element` dependency or by writing it themselves.

To help with this, the `register-elements` package includes `@guardian/flex-model-to-prosemirror` as an external dependency. 

The transformation out, ie from `externalDomain` to `internal`, is defined in a `transformMap`, with a structure that looks like an `internal` to `externalDomain` (see example below).

Here’s an example of transforming some `Domain` types, in `register-elements`, to `internal`.

### `transformMap`

Each of our transformmaps is a `Map` that has a key-value pair, where the key is of type `Internal`, and the value is of type `External`.

```js
// Example from [transformMap.json](https://github.com/DFE-Digital/register-elements/tree/master/packages/register-elements/src/data/transformMaps):
const { TRANSFORMS_MAP } = require('../data/transformMaps');
```

```js
// Example of a transform map
const transformMap = {
    'Domain.TeacherId': 'ID',
    'Domain.OrganisationId': 'ID',
    'Domain.RefCode': 'STRING',
    'Domain.TeacherGrade': 'STRING',
    'Domain.Salary': (x) => x / 100.00

## Decision: ### We will change our main hash function to SHA256

SHA256 and RIPEMD160 both provide the same security level and are roughly equivalent,
except that RIPEMD160 is backwards compatible while SHA256 is not.
A practical concern is that SHA256 is not a hash of a public key and therefore is not suitable
for signing.

##### Addressing the concerns

- The implementation is not drastically different and should be relatively easy
- There has already been an effort to replace all occurrences of RIPEMD160 with SHA256 (see https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/pull/4414)
- A formal security review should be scheduled. The developers are available over the next month.
- An updated specification should be made. We will coordinate with the devs.
- Dependencies, interface definitions, and such should be updated by the Tendermint team.
  This is not done in Tendermint's repository and we would be unable to test or verify the fixes.

#### Why not use a modern standard?

While SHA3 and Blake2 are modern hash functions and are generally preferred over SHA256,
they also have a larger sized digests (32 vs 224 bits). The trade-off for SHA3 is not significant
given we're already having to manage RAM use and memory footprint.
Furthermore, SHA3 does not provide a drop-in replacement for SHA256 in the code we have.
It is simply a different hashing scheme with the same security level.

##### We will keep using RIPEMD160 and ED25519

There doesn't appear to be a significant threat model for using these even in production environments.
Given they provide identical security level to the hash functions but in a smaller footprint,
the risks are relatively low.

#### In summary

While SHA256 and Blake2 provide identical security levels, it is better to stick to established and trusted hashing algorithms.
We already have an established pipeline for these algorithms in Tendermint, and all other projects and libraries would work with them.

SHA3 is great, but we can not drop our dependencies and all the development work we would need to do to drop them is too much work for too little gain.

## Decision: * **Immutability is consistent with the intended use case**: Immutable data is generally intended to be passed in to functions/methods that are highly pure (ie: they don't mutate their arguments)
* **Immutability simplifies implementation**: No need to worry about reference equality issues that can crop up with mutable data. "Is this data new?" is the only thing that matters, not "is this data shared by other references?"
* **Immutability enables non-destructive transformations**: Functions/methods can modify _references_ to data without altering the data itself.
* **Immutability simplifies serialisation**: Because everything is by reference, you don't need special serialization implementations for immutable objects.
* **Immutability improves performance**: The object reference is not a replica or duplicate of data, so the object references are less expensive to store.
* **Immutability is more difficult to compromise**: It's generally difficult to make an immutable object "dirty".
* **Immutability is easier to use in functional programming styles**: Immutable objects lend themselves to "reduce and conquer" algorithms that can use functional style operations.
* **Immutability is safer**: Immutable objects are impossible to modify except at the point of construction.
* **Immutability is more resilient to concurrency issues**: Since there's no mutable data to de-order during concurrent requests, immutability offers a number of advantages in a concurrent environment.
* **Immutability is compatible with the functional style programming paradigm**: Functional programming is inherently about building new objects rather than modifying existing ones.
* **Immutability allows for a more functional approach to computer science**: There are many possible programming languages, and we don't need to conform to the "object orientation" dogma that many people seem to be clinging to.

## Decision: - The CMp Digital Platform
    - A 24-36 month old Cloud Infrastructure and Service provider, managed by Crown Marketplace
    - An "in-house tool" for government services, designed by Digital Marketplace
  
### Why the CMp Digital Platform?
- Less maintenance for suppliers of government services, as they get the tools from the service and can access them all
- Common platform helps with platform maintenance, development and support
- Common infrastructure reduces the "learning curve" for the first phase
- We don't know any more about the future needs than we already anticipate, and it's possible that we will need more powerful infrastructure which may or not be available in AWS/Azure
- We have an example we can follow (CCS Travel and DigiTS), which would be beneficial
- Will provide value even if our infrastructure needs are small - by building out the platform we ensure that other services can benefit, and can also take the easiest routes
- We would be helping to reduce the maintenance of the tools themselves, as the CMp Digital Platform team could make improvements of their infrastructure, and support all of the users from a single platform.

### How should the CMp Digital Platform be provisioned?
A new CMp Digital Platform environment will need to be provisioned, with the Digital Outcome and Specialists framework
  
- New CMp Digital Platform provisioning and development environments, and all users of the CMp Digital Platform
- Development environments, and users of those environments.
- DigiTS environment (the 'existing' CMp Digital Platform)
- Facilities Management environments.

### What approach should we take?
We will use the CMp Digital Platform development environments in the construction of all new services,
and the Production environments for operational systems.

However we must be careful not to duplicate any work that the Facilities Management will undertake.
In addition, we can make a greater-than-100% contribution to that development and make available more than one environments to that framework.
We will need to discuss the best way to avoid work duplication and ensure that a single environment is available for our development needs.

#### Environments in our infrastructure

We should aim to create new environments as we make new services, and should not duplicate or share environments.
  
Our pipeline would have a dedicated 'production' environment which would run the services under the production environment of the CMp Digital Platform.

## Decision: * We need a way to tell the `kubelet` to reach the `registry-buddy` to enable automated health checks.
* We need a way to tell the `kubelet` to only attempt to connect the `registry-buddy` in the context of a trusted workload (`cf-api-server`, `cf-api-worker`).
* We need a way to verify the `registry-buddy` doesn't offer any other functionality beyond the liveness probe.

### Local Liveness Probe

A liveness probe using an HTTP request to an existing endpoint on the `registry-buddy` is implemented. Each `Pod` has a config
resource in a pod-specific namespace to be built and mounted to the `registry-buddy`. This resource will be built and pushed by
a CI/CD job configured for the `registry-buddy` to host.

This probe will be attempted by the `kubelet` only on trusted workloads. The kubelet should be able to reach this endpoint
since the pod would be.

### Health Endpoint Endpoint

An HTTP request health endpoint is configured by a Pod in the `registry-buddy` namespace as described above. Each `Pod`
should be built and pushed by a CI/CD job configured for the `registry-buddy`.

The `kubelet` will make HTTP requests to this endpoint on the `registry-buddy` by trusted workloads.

# [Pros/cons of transformations and minification](0005-build-phase-transformation-and-minification.md)

**Transformation (from ESM to CJS) has the following benefits.**

- Dependency management
- Support for `import`
- Support for `export` (all code)
- Support for `export * as` (all code)

[Minification] removes unnecessary characters for packaging and deployment.

[Minification] does not affect code distribution (compared with transformation).

[Minification] has no effect on dependency management.

[Minification] has no effect on code distribution.

**Transformation (from ESM to CJS) has the following downsides.**

- Dependencies can be affected by the transformation
- Modules can be affected by the transformation
- Code distribution can be affected by the transformation

[Minification] has a similar, but smaller set of downsides, since it replaces characters as well.
