## Decision: ### Commits must be signed by two trusted developers

The delivery pipeline will reject PRs which have not been signed by at least two
trusted developers in addition to the author of the PR. 

The pipeline will accept PRs signed by only a single developer after verification
with the trusted developers.

### Authorised developers

For the purpose of this ADR, an "authorised developer" is a member of the
[Core Team](https://core-team.github.io/).

### Disallowed users

In addition to the authorised developers, the following users and organisations
are not authorised:

1. members of the public;
2. any organisation not on the Core Team (e.g. a contributor organisation);
3. any organisation which is a competitor.

### Usage of Git API

The delivery pipeline will make use of the GitHub API to reject PRs authored by
members of the public and those from organisations which are competitors.

The delivery pipeline will use the WebAuth API to ensure that the pipeline is
not being used to make changes to repositories by an unauthorised user. The
pipeline will require a combination of the `public_repo` and `write` roles.

The delivery pipeline will use the [webops-api](https://github.com/FluxLabs/webops-api)

be vulnerable to false positives if a key is present in an environment.

## Decision: * Chosen Alternative: Wrap test execution in a database transaction.
    * Rollback transactions can only be used with PostgreSQL. Other databases we are testing against can not be wrapped in a transaction.
    * **In memory tests** are still possible with the wrap approach. Each memory-backed test run will set up its own transaction, and each will have a `TRUNCATE` command after its test.
    * Wrap tests in transactions will execute as reliable tests that do not cause data-race situations, since each test's data will never be affected by a previous test.
    * Wrap tests in transactions are more sensitive to test failure. While they can succeed in their own isolation, failing to execute all tests in a transaction will cause all tests to fail, even if a number of tests pass.
* *Test run duration:* This tests runs slightly longer as it must clean up after each test.

* *Developer experience:* The developer will be more familiar with test execution workflows where the cleanup happens automatically. We can add a comment to each test in this style, demonstrating the intent of the code.

* *Priorities:* In order of our desired outcomes:

1. Reliable tests
1. Developer experience
1. Minimizing test run duration

## Decision: We will use a Google Cloud Function, in the file storage service, but not in
the web service's URL (so that we make it difficult for attackers to
mal-use the Google Cloud Function for sending HTTP request data) to perform
the work of downloading and comparing the file metadata checksums.

### Details

The idea is to use a separate set of Cloud Function (CF) instances dedicated
solely to file integrity protection. In this way we can have
multiple CF instances all working simultaneously.

There will be two groups CFs:

1. The "main" CFs will run within the web service's IP range (and hence
   its network address), so that the CF can tell us about certain known
   file names (if, for example, the CF is running the FileStream service).
2. The "watchdog" CFs will run in an isolated network segment (probably a
   virtual machine or a container running outside the web service). They
   will allow us to add more machines to the work, all concurrently.

The advantage of running some CFs in a different IP range is to make it
difficult for attackers to use the CF for other purposes. So, for instance,
if we set the file checksum metadata in a file that is outside the web
service's reach, the web service cannot benefit from the information contained
in the file checksum. However, as the "main" CFs live within the web
service's network, they can reach all of our objects, and benefit from the
information contained in the metadata.

## Decision: In the context of the 5 phases of the data lifecycle, and the temporal requirements on the data, we will apply a retention policy that ensures that 
a. the data is available as and when required
b. the data is deleted according to the deletion policy after a specified retention period.
c. GDPR requirements on the retention and destruction of personal data are met.
d. General Data Protection regulation (GDPR) requirements are met.

The retention policy is that we will store each data item within a 6 hour (0.5 hours in case of non-personal data, and 6 hours for personal data) range of time.
The retention policy is that we will purge each data item after a specified period of time.
That period of time will be 
	a. 30 days for business data
	b. 18 months for financial data
	c. 3 years for archival data
	d. 10 years for record-keeping.
That decision will be based on the following matrix:
- business need
- need to retain access to the data
- compliance with retention requirements
- impact of possible data loss on activities

The retention policy will only apply to:
- Data items loaded using the Datahike loader
- Data items which are loaded through the CLI or API
- Data items loaded during ingest

This policy does not relate to data that is already part of the Datahike system, but to all data that is created by means of the Datahike loader, either loaded during ingest, or loaded at another time, but to be stored until 
its life cycle is over.

We will apply the retention policy to new data loaded starting from today.
For all existing data loaded in the past, the datahike system will not know the retention policy. 
Those data will be in the system and should be managed in the same way as other data that arrives today.
The retention policy is that we will purge each data item after a specified period of time.
That period of time will be:
	a. 30 days for business data
	b. 18 months for financial data
	c. 3 years for archival data
	d. 10 years for record-keeping

An automated purge process will be established to remove data after the specified period of time.

## Decision: ### The Aggregate Has Its Own State

An aggregate has its own distinct state from its parent process. Updates to the
state must come from the process.

Because we want to maintain backwards compatability, we will not store a
previous value of the state. Previously the state of an aggregate was
available by checking the state of a related entity.

### Only One Property Is Set At Creation

When constructing an aggregate we will only ever set the `value` property.
The property set is used by the process and the aggregate API as a reference to
the aggregate's instance state.

### Property Names

Each of the following names will also be used in an aggregate's instance state:
`id`, `created`, `updated`, and `deleted`.

Each of the following names will also be used as a property of an aggregate
object:
`state` (which will store the value of the aggregate's instance state),
`stateChanges` (which will store all changes of the aggregate's instance state,
see ADR-17).

### Properties That Are Not Set

When constructing an aggregate, we will set the following properties to null:
`value`, `state`.

## Decision: We have decided to run as 3-machine kubernetes cluster and we will run GlusterFS volume
type to ensure we mount the volumes to the pods. We ruled out using Rook because
of the complexity involved in preparing for use and because we decided to focus
using kubernetes cluster to be run in just Kubernetes clusters.

We have ruled out using NFS because if we were to mount NFS volumes into containers
then we would need to mount them as Read Write Many, and NFS does not allow
multiple mount points. This would, effectively, allow mounting a single NFS volume
into multiple containers at a single time.
We have ruled out using GlusterFS as it is really not that stable, and has
no stable release yet as I write this (2021). It also requires enabling a lot
of features and requires some amount of work to get working in a stable way.

We have decided to use a file volume type because it does not provide all the
features. NFS does not allow multiple mount point. GlusterFS mount points are
only in one direction (mount from host/glusterfs to multiple containers). Also
seems that multiple mounts in same host from multiple containers are not allowed.
On the other hand, we can't mount a host volume using RFS, and we wanted to use
the read-write-many approach anyway.

## Decision: We designed a mechanism to allow the library `flutter_downloader` work in background and add all tasks into download queue.
These functionalities are not available upon `Unsplash.dart` since Flutter task manager have no built-in support of `WorkManager`.
`Unsplash` would be only the first library from its set.
The other task manager supported by `Unsplash` are `WorkManager`, `Dex` and `TaskRunner`.
"WorkManager" is the name for it by default since it is the most versatile of its set, built upon the needs of the Android market.
`WorkManager` can do all the different things for multiple apps (eg download a File and upload, extract the File, move to destination) for each of a set of Tasks.
`Dex` uses a daemon approach (background worker) while `TaskRunner` is a more modular Android task manager that would execute tasks concurrently.
`Unsplash` already adds `Dex` to the set of its supporting task manager.
Unsplash in Android is very common (at least in Android development community) so to increase the probability of Android library compatibility, we should support the most versatile Android task manager.
WorkManager by google has good integration, it's well maintained, it can handle multiple downloads and the URL provided has to be an absolute URL, http or https.

Download task is the same as file save task so the logic will be the same :

1. Do the downloading

```js
double downloadTask(String url, String saveDir, int priority, Api call, SendFileSendType upload)
```

2. Start the download process

```js
void download(String url, String saveDir, int priority, Api call, SendFileSendType upload)
```

3. Cancel the download process

```js
void downloadCancel(String url, String saveDir, int priority, Api call, SendFileSendType upload)
```

4. Get the download progress

```js
double downloadProgress(String url, String saveDir, int priority, Api call, SendFileSendType upload)
```

5. Get the download status (progress, success, failure)

```js
double downloadStatus(String url, String saveDir, int priority, Api call, SendFileSendType upload)
```

## Decision: ### App architecture
Inspired by WorkManager and Google Worker, this lib would make it easier to design the app architecture. App execution flows via queues which are ordered in collections. Therefore, this architecture is built around this notion.
This application architecture offers 7 important benefits:
- WorkManager is an open source
- It also is easily installed, very small footprint
- Is designed from the ground up for running tasks in the background
- Has the concept of queues and run-times
- Runtimes can be set to any time, including start time after the lifecycle of a fragment and also with system/application lifecycle
- Should be compatible with most IDEs
- Interlocks with the application's lifecycle
- Allows shutdown of all jobs with system or application shutdown
- Guarantees that no job will be interrupted, rescheduled or blocked by the lifecycle
- Allows creation of multiple job queues
- Also, the main thread can act as queue in case of no more background execution. So it is not an excessive overhead
- To safeguard against CPU or service starvation, this architecture allows setting a limit to the number of runs of the same task.
- The architecture is set up to maximize developer flexibility
- Also allows integration of external job providers, such as cronjob
- Will be as easy to integrate as WorkManager itself
- Supports periodic, asynchronous jobs from all system and application lifecycles
- Jobs in the queue will be automatically rescheduled in case of process/application shutdown
- Supports chained jobs: the output of one job is the input of another. In the event that the job is interrupted, the scheduler should resume it or run it in parallel
- We can only use the `WorkManager` API.

## Decision: Chosen option: "Grouping with numbers in the names", because

- the "grouping" is just the katas naming and grouping numbers, not a real grouping in the "global katas organization tree", since any katas name can be grouped to katas in any other number, like katas 109 as katas 110, katas 110 as katas 119 and so on.

## Decision: 1. New files of every data element have all of their information in it (ie. all of the metadata); there is one configuration file

8. There need to be some constraints on the data configuration that's possible from a programmatic/syntactical point of view; for example, you must provide type information, a key field, parent, and (for XML) type.
